findings.evidence:
The Stripe client is deleted and replaced by the Paylane client in the same
release. There is no switch between the two: keeping both would double the
code to maintain. The Stripe account is closed the day after the release.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: All traffic moves at deploy
findings.recommendation: If Paylane fails in production after the release (authorizations rejected, outage, captures not settling), redeploying the previous version does not restore payments: the Stripe account is already closed the next day, so checkout stays broken with no rollback. Keep the Stripe client behind a configuration switch (provider selected per environment) and keep the Stripe account open until Paylane has run in production for an agreed period; decide the rollback path in the design and add a task for it.
findings.title: The switch to Paylane has no way back

findings.evidence:
A new worker, `settlement-worker`, runs at 02:00, fetches the day's Paylane
payments and matches them to orders. It runs as a Kubernetes CronJob and
writes its result to the database.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: A worker settles payments nightly
findings.recommendation: If the CronJob fails, is not scheduled, or cannot reach Paylane at 02:00, the only output is a database write that never happens: the spec alerts finance only for an unmatched payment, so a night with no settlement at all goes unnoticed until someone checks the books. Decide in the design how the worker reports a run — a log at start and end with the run's counts, a metric or last-success timestamp, and an alert when a night's run fails or does not complete — and add it to task 1.2.
findings.title: Nobody would see the settlement worker fail
